title: Assignment 5: Government Data Scraping Report
text: The objective of this assignment was to automate the collection of government documents using R. Specifically, the task involved searching GovInfo for documents related to the Foreign Relations Committee, downloading the ten most recent results, and storing them for analysis.

title: Assignment 5: Government Data Scraping Report
text:
A. The Scraping Process
I utilized a provided R script (govtdata01.R) which processes a JSON/CSV list of search results. The script utilizes the purrr package to iterate through file URLs and download.file to save the PDFs locally.
Key steps taken in the script:

Loaded Libraries: purrr, magrittr, jsonlite, and dplyr.
Input Data: Read the search results containing metadata (PDF links and Package IDs).
Directory Setup: Created the target folder assignments/assign05.
Execution: Ran a loop restricted to 1:10 to capture only the ten most recent files.



Code
# Snippet of the download logic used
results <- 1:10 %>% 
  purrr::map_chr(~ download_govfiles_pdf(pdf_govfiles_url[.], pdf_govfiles_id[.]))

title: Assignment 5: Government Data Scraping Report
text:
B. Difficulties Encountered
During the scraping process, several challenges emerged:

Dynamic URLs: The links provided in the search export are sometimes temporary or session-based. If too much time passes between the search and the download script execution, the links may expire.
Anti-Scraping Measures: Government servers often have rate limits. While Sys.sleep(runif(1, 1, 3)) was used to mimic human behavior, running a larger batch (e.g., 100+ files) could still trigger IP bans or timeouts.
File Naming: The default filenames (based on packageId or index) are not descriptive (e.g., govfiles_1.pdf). This makes it difficult to know what the document is without opening it.

title: Assignment 5: Government Data Scraping Report
text:
C. Usability and Improvement

1. How usable is the scraped data?
The scraped data consists of unstructured PDF files. * Pros: They are the official, authoritative source documents. * Cons: They are not immediately “computable.” You cannot easily run regressions or frequency counts on them without a secondary processing step (OCR or text extraction). Furthermore, metadata (dates, authors) is locked inside the PDF text rather than being in a tidy dataframe.


2. How to improve?
To make this process robust for a larger research project, I would recommend:

Use the API: Instead of manually downloading a CSV search result and feeding it to R, use the GovInfo API. This allows for dynamic querying and ensures links are fresh.
Text Extraction: Integrate the pdftools package in R to immediately convert the downloaded PDFs into text strings.
Metadata Enrichment: Rename the files using the title or date columns from the CSV during the download loop (e.g., 2024-11-27_Hearing_Transcript.pdf) to improve organization.

title: Assignment 3: Mapping Census Data — Median Rent & SNAP in Washington Counties
text:
What I Learned (Interpretation)

Median rent is highest in/near large urban counties, while many rural counties show lower rents—consistent with stronger demand and tighter housing markets around cities.
The SNAP tables reflect population size as much as need: large counties (e.g., King) naturally have more SNAP households in absolute numbers. To compare reliance, a rate (e.g., % of households with SNAP) would be more informative than a raw count.
Margins of error vary widely; smaller counties often have relatively larger MOEs, reminding me that ACS is a survey and precision differs by place/size.

title: Assignment 1: Website Design Note
text:
Overview
This website is created using RStudio Quarto and deployed to GitHub Pages. Quarto provides a clean, reproducible workflow where site-wide options (title, navbar, theme, and table of contents) are managed in _quarto.yml, and content pages are authored in portable .qmd files.


Visual Design

Theme: I use the cosmo theme for a professional, readable look with strong defaults for typography and spacing.
Consistency: A single custom stylesheet styles.css applies light tweaks while preserving theme consistency.
Readability: The table of contents (TOC) is enabled on longer pages to aid scanning and navigation.



Navigation & Information Architecture
The navigation bar connects visitors to the site’s core areas: 1. Home (index.qmd) – brief introduction and purpose. 2. About (about.qmd) – short bio and contact. 3. Assignments (dropdown) – coursework organized by assignment (this page is under Assignment 1). 4. Resume/CV – a direct link to my updated resume PDF for quick access.
This structure keeps coursework easy to find while also presenting my profile information and credentials.


Technical Setup

Authoring: .qmd files (Quarto Markdown) support standard Markdown and optional code chunks when needed.
Configuration: _quarto.yml centralizes the site’s title, navbar, theme, TOC, and custom CSS.
Build & Preview: I use quarto render and quarto preview locally to test layout and links.
Deployment: Publishing is done to GitHub Pages, which serves the site at https://<username>.github.io.



Rationale & Future Enhancements
The goal is a clean, professional, and low-maintenance site. Quarto’s structure keeps content organized, while the cosmo theme ensures a cohesive visual style. Future improvements may include a Projects/Portfolio page, tags for posts, a light/dark mode toggle, and simple analytics.
Summary: Built with RStudio Quarto using the cosmo theme, this site features clear navigation (Home, About, Assignments, Resume/CV) that connects readers to my content and credentials in a straightforward, professional way.

title: About Me
text:
Hi! I’m Nedret Sen Cavus, and this fall I’m beginning my Master of Science in Social Data Analytics and Research at The University of Texas at Dallas — the next step toward my dream of earning a PhD in Social Psychology and becoming a researcher–professor.
I’ve always been fascinated by how people think, feel, and act toward others — especially when group identities, social inequalities, and crisis situations are involved. My passion lies in understanding intergroup relations, social injustice, and how social identity shapes prosocial behavior.
I hold a B.A. in Psychology (Cum Laude) from Hacettepe University, and during my undergrad I spent six months at Radboud University in the Netherlands through the Erasmus+ exchange program, focusing on intergroup relations and prosocial/antisocial behavior.
I’ve also worked as a Graduate Research Assistant in Prof. Linda Tropp’s Intergroup Relations & Social Justice Lab at the University of Massachusetts Amherst, where I helped design research projects, collect and analyze data (ANOVA, regression, correlations), and explore ways to promote social cohesion between diverse groups.
Beyond the academic details, I’m someone who:
Loves diving into books and new research articles
Thrives in collaborative, idea-driven environments

title: Assignment 2: Google Trends Data Analysis Comparison with R
text:
To examine search interest related to the 2024 U.S. presidential election, I collected Google Trends data for the search terms Trump, Kamala Harris, and Election using two approaches:

Google Trends Website On the Google Trends website, I entered the three terms, set the location to the United States, and chose the custom time interval January 15, 2024 to December 17, 2024. This range covers the election process from the early primaries through Election Day. I downloaded the dataset as a CSV file.
R with gtrendsR Package I installed and loaded the gtrendsR package in RStudio. Using the custom time range option, I ran:
library(gtrendsR)

TrumpHarrisElection <- gtrends(
  c("Trump", "Harris", "election"),
  geo = "US",
  gprop = "web",
  time = "2024-01-15 2024-12-17",
  onlyInterest = TRUE
)

the_df <- TrumpHarrisElection$interest_over_time
write.csv(the_df, "TrumpHarrisElection.csv", row.names = FALSE)
save(the_df, file = "TrumpHarrisElection.RData")
This produced both CSV and RData files in my working directory.

title: Assignment 2: Google Trends Data Analysis Comparison with R
text:
R Plot



B. Data Characteristics

Dates and Intervals: For this eleven-month window, Google Trends aggregated the data by week. Each record shows the relative interest score (0–100) for a keyword in that week.
Variables:

Website: CSV in wide format (columns for “Trump,” “Harris,” “Election”).
R: Long format dataframe (columns include “date,” “hits,” “keyword”), which is easier to use programmatically.





C. Observed Interest Patterns
When reviewing the data, several clear patterns emerged:

Trump maintained consistently high search interest throughout 2024, often spiking around debates, major rallies, or controversial news stories.
Harris showed lower baseline interest compared to Trump, but her search volume rose sharply during key campaign events, especially after the Democratic National Convention and during the final weeks before the election.
Election as a search term followed the expected seasonal curve: modest early in the year, steadily increasing during the summer and fall, and peaking in early November around Election Day (Nov 5, 2024).

Overall, the patterns align with the media cycle: candidate-specific terms fluctuated depending on news coverage, while the general term “election” built momentum toward the decisive date.



D. Comparison of the Two Methods

Format of Data

Website: Wide format, better for manual inspection in Excel.
R: Long format, better for coding and reshaping.

Flexibility

Website: Manual and intuitive but limited.
R: Scriptable, reproducible, and allows more terms or time ranges to be added easily.

Granularity

Website: Gave weekly data for this range, with daily possible for shorter spans.
R: Same rules as Google’s API; in this case, also weekly.

Output Options

Website: Only CSV.
R: CSV, RData, and other formats directly usable in R.

Ease of Use

Website: Quick and user-friendly.
R: Requires setup but far more efficient for repeated analysis.





E. Conclusion

Website: Fast, visual, perfect for a quick figure or sanity check.
R (gtrendsR): Reproducible, auditable, scalable, and better suited for serious data production & collection. You get tidy data, extra tables (regions, related queries), and full control over cleaning and analysis.

For this assignment, both routes produced consistent weekly series over the same 2024 window. The methodological advantages—reproducibility, parameter tracking, and scale—clearly favor R for research-grade work, while the website excels at quick exploration and presentation.

1. Foreign-Exchange Reserves

#Reading the HTML code from the Wiki website

2. Life Expectancy
This table required selecting specific columns for overall, female, and male life expectancy. I calculated the gender gap (Female - Male) to add analytical value.


Code
url_life <- "https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_by_life_expectancy"
wiki_life <- read_html(url_life)

life_df <- wiki_life %>%
  html_element("table.wikitable") %>%
  html_table(fill = TRUE)

# Remove the first row. It contains sub-headers like "at birth" 
life_df <- life_df[-1, ] 

# Select specific columns by index based on the 2023 UN table structure:
# Col 1: Country
# Col 2: Overall (at birth)
# Col 12: Female (at birth) - (Skipping 4 age columns and the Male block)
# Col 7: Male (at birth)   - (Skipping 4 age columns)
life_df <- life_df[, c(1, 2, 12, 7)]

names(life_df) <- c("Country", "Overall", "Female", "Male")

life_df <- life_df %>%
  mutate(
    Country = str_split_fixed(Country, "\\[", 2)[, 1],
    Overall = str_split_fixed(Overall, "\\[", 2)[, 1],
    Female  = str_split_fixed(Female, "\\[", 2)[, 1],
    Male    = str_split_fixed(Male, "\\[", 2)[, 1]
  )

# Convert to numeric (This should now work without warnings)
life_df$Overall <- as.numeric(life_df$Overall)
life_df$Female  <- as.numeric(life_df$Female)
life_df$Male    <- as.numeric(life_df$Male)

# 3. Calculate & Filter
life_df$Gender_Gap <- life_df$Female - life_df$Male

life_df <- life_df %>%
  filter(!is.na(Country), Country != "World") %>%
  arrange(desc(Overall))

# 4. Save
write.csv(life_df, "life_expectancy_clean.csv", row.names = FALSE)
message("Life Expectancy Scraped: ", nrow(life_df), " countries.")

title: Assignment 4: Webscraping 1 with R (rvest)
text:
C. Data Plan for Research
Acquiring web data for research requires a robust and ethical “Data Plan.” If I were to scale this project, I would follow these steps:

Source Verification & Ethics:

Check robots.txt (e.g., wikipedia.org/robots.txt) to ensure scraping is permitted.
Prioritize official APIs (e.g., World Bank API) over scraping HTML, as HTML structure is brittle and changes frequently.

Data Pipeline:

Raw Storage: Always save the raw HTML or JSON responses immediately (writeLines or saveRDS). This allows re-parsing later without re-pinging the server.
Cleaning Layer: Use the functions developed above (safe_parse_num, ensure_country_col) to normalize data types immediately.
Validation: Implement tests (e.g., “Does every row have a Country?”, “Are reserves > 0?”) to flag scraping errors automatically.

Maintenance:

Wikipedia tables often change IDs or column orders. Code should be written to find columns by name (using matches()), not by index position (e.g., df[,5]), to prevent breakage when columns move.

title: Assignment 6: Text Analysis with Quanteda
text:
A. Biden-Xi Summit Analysis
I utilized Latent Semantic Analysis (LSA) and network plots to understand the structure of tweets regarding the Biden-Xi summit.


Code
library(quanteda)
library(quanteda.textmodels)
library(quanteda.textplots)
library(quanteda.textstats)
library(readr)
library(ggplot2)
library(tidyverse)

# Load Data
summit <- read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/datageneration/datamethods/master/textanalytics/summit_11162021.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
sum_twt <- summit$text


The analysis of hashtags reveals the primary topics of conversation. Co-occurrence networks show which tags frequently appear together.


Code
# Create DFM and select hashtags
tweet_dfm <- tokens(sum_twt, remove_punct = TRUE) |> dfm()
tag_dfm <- dfm_select(tweet_dfm, pattern = "#*")
toptag <- names(topfeatures(tag_dfm, 50))

# Create FCM and Plot
tag_fcm <- fcm(tag_dfm)
topgat_fcm <- fcm_select(tag_fcm, pattern = toptag)

textplot_network(topgat_fcm, min_freq = 50, edge_alpha = 0.8, edge_size = 1, vertex_size = 3)









Observation: The network highlights clusters around #biden, #xi, and #china, with secondary clusters focusing on specific policy issues like #taiwan and #trade.

title: Assignment 6: Text Analysis with Quanteda
text:
B. US Presidential Inaugural Speeches
Using the data_corpus_inaugural dataset, I analyzed shifts in rhetoric over time.

1. Keyness Analysis: Trump vs. Obama
I compared the 2017 (Trump) and 2009/2013 (Obama) inaugural addresses using “Keyness.” This statistical measure identifies words that are highly distinctive to one document set compared to another.


Code
# Subset Corpus
pres_corpus <- corpus_subset(data_corpus_inaugural, President %in% c("Obama", "Trump"))
pres_dfm <- tokens(pres_corpus, remove_punct = TRUE) |>
  tokens_remove(stopwords("english")) |>
  tokens_group(groups = President) |>
  dfm()

# Calculate Keyness (Target: Trump)
result_keyness <- textstat_keyness(pres_dfm, target = "Trump")
textplot_keyness(result_keyness, show_reference = TRUE)









Interpretation:

Trump (Right/Blue): distinctively used words like “America”, “first”, “borders”, and “wealth”. This reflects a nationalist, protectionist rhetoric.
Obama (Left/Grey): distinctively used words like “journey”, “generation”, “peace”, and “crisis”. This reflects a rhetoric focused on continuity, narrative progress, and abstract ideals.



2. Temporal Analysis (X-Ray Plot)
To visualize how specific terms fluctuate over time, I created “X-Ray” dispersion plots for the post-1949 era.


Code
# Subset Post-1949
data_corpus_recent <- corpus_subset(data_corpus_inaugural, Year > 1949)
kwic_american <- kwic(tokens(data_corpus_recent), pattern = "american")
kwic_communist <- kwic(tokens(data_corpus_recent), pattern = "communist")

textplot_xray(kwic_american, kwic_communist)









Interpretation: The term “American” remains a consistently high-frequency term across all modern presidents.

title: Assignment 6: Text Analysis with Quanteda
text:
C. Wordfish Analysis

1. What is Wordfish?
Based on my research on the quanteda website: Wordfish is an unsupervised text scaling model. Unlike “Wordscores” (which requires reference texts with known scores), Wordfish estimates the positions of documents solely based on word frequencies. It assumes that word usage follows a Poisson distribution and extracts a single dimension of variation (often interpreted as left-right ideology or populism vs. establishment).


2. Application to Inaugural Speeches
I applied Wordfish to speeches from 1980 to the present to estimate the rhetorical positions of recent presidents.


Code
# Create DFM for recent speeches (1980-Present)
recent_corpus <- corpus_subset(data_corpus_inaugural, Year >= 1980)
recent_dfm <- tokens(recent_corpus, remove_punct = TRUE) |>
  tokens_remove(stopwords("english")) |>
  dfm()

# Run Wordfish
# Dirichlet Initialization helps separate the poles
wf_model <- textmodel_wordfish(recent_dfm, dir = c(1, 9)) 

# Plot
textplot_scale1d(wf_model) +
  labs(title = "Wordfish Scaling of Recent Presidents (1980-Present)",
       x = "Estimated Position (Theta)",
       y = "President") +
  theme_minimal()









Conclusion: The Wordfish model successfully places the presidents along a latent dimension. The visualization allows us to see how “close” or “distant” the rhetoric of one president is from another based purely on their vocabulary choices.
